catalog_quote: Since Mathevet did not mark stress, we must turn to other sources, one external and one internal, to determine the stress pattern of Nipmuck. The PA Alternating Stress Rule provides the external source, and a basis from which to begin the analysis of Nipmuck. In PA, every long vowel, and every other short vowel (starting from the left of the word) receives stress (Aubin 1980). For the most part, Ojibwe retains this stress pattern, as in the following examples, in which the stressed vowels are underlined: *masenahikanali > Oj. mazina?iganan 'books' ... In the first word, every other vowel is stressed in both Ojibwe and PA, since all the vowels are short. In the second word, every long vowel and every short vowel (starting at the beginning of the word, and then restarting after a long vowel) is stressed. ... audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim on printed p. 37 of the held thesis PDF (page image opened). The deciding source is the only grammar of the language and is held; but the stress statement itself is a comparative inference (PA Alternating Stress Rule projected onto an 18th-c. manuscript that marks no stress, supported by syncope), so the record can never be better than hedged -- 'thin' by nature of the evidence, not by neglect, and the existing QS-HEDGED / weight-hedged coding already reflects that. The two open specialist papers fetched sources now (Costa 2007, Goddard 2016) are silent on a Loup stress rule; Costa's remarks on metrically conditioned syncope in SNEA are compatible with Gustafson. One caution worth carrying in the record's idn/caution field (not a recode): Goddard 2016 argues the Loup A manuscript mixes three distinct SNEA varieties (Loup 1-3), so 'Nipmuck' as a single-language label for M

sources.citation: Goddard, Ives. 2016 [conf. 2012]. The 'Loup' languages of Western Massachusetts: the dialectal diversity of Southern New England Algonquian. Papers of the 44th Algonquian Conference, 104-138.
sources.quote: None. Only incidental: 'The retention of word-final unstressed voiced syllables in Loup 3 and 4 ... makes these languages exceptional within SNEA' (p. 121). Identity note: 'Verbal inflections thus point to the existence of three distinct languages that are represented in the Loup A manuscript' (p. 106-107).
sources.locator: pp. 105-107 (Loup A manuscript = three distinct varieties, Loup 1/2/3); p. 121 (retention of word-final unstressed syllables in Loup 3); no stress rule stated

sources.citation: Costa, David J. 2007. The dialectology of Southern New England Algonquian. Papers of the 38th Algonquian Conference, 81-127.
sources.quote: No Loup stress rule. 'Abenaki Syncope is only sporadic in Loup and Narragansett' (p. 98); conditioning of syncope in SNEA 'seems to depend on currently ill-understood metrical factors' (fn. 72); in Massachusett syncope is triggered 'when the syllable in question is odd numbered or follows a long vowel' (p. 98).
